To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

exfoliative toxin cleaves the desmosomal adhesion molecule Dsg1, which leads to a loss of cell-cell adhesion and skin blistering, and we have identified the mechanism by which Dsg1 cleaves leads to skin blistering.

the blister-inducing exfoliative toxin cleaves desmoglein-1, a desmosomal protein that mediates epidermal adhesion, and that plakoglobin, a protein partner of desmoglein, rescues the loss of adhesiveness caused by exfoliative toxin.
ectodomain-truncated desmoglein-1 (Dsg) disrupts desmosomal function and induces blistering in a manner dependent on plakoglobin sequestering.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the pathogenesis of the blistering diseases staphylococcus scalded-skinsyndrome (SSSS) and bullous impetio (BI).
the molecular mechanisms of skin adhesion, and how these mechanisms are disrupted in blistering diseases.
the molecular mechanisms that underlie the development of skin blistering in the human skin diseases bullous impetoigo and staphycococcal scaldyed-skin syndrome.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the exfoliative toxin cleaves the ectodomain of desmoglein-1, a protein that is critical for the adhesion of keratinocytes, and that the resulting loss of desmogle-1 function is the cause of the blistering.
plakoglobin is a crucial component in maintaining desmosomal adhesion and its sequestration by ectodomain-depleted desmoglein1 leads to a loss of desmosomal function.

the loss of Dsg1 ectodomains by exfoliative toxin cleavage leads to a reduction in the expression levels of endogenous Dsg1 and other cadherins in desmosomes and the loss of adhesiveness of the keratinocyte sheets, which is prevented by increasing plakoglobin expression.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
plakoglobin rescues the adhesive defects induced by exfoliative toxin and ectodomain truncations of desmoglein.
the ectodomain-truncated desmosomal cadhernin desmogleins (Dsg) 1 is a pathogenic molecule that can disrupt desmosomes and cause skin blistering.
the ectodomain of Dsg1 is essential to its function in desmosomes, that ectodomain truncations of Dsg1 disrupt adhesion, and that plakoglobin is required for these effects.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the desmosomal protein plakoglobin can be used as a target for the development of therapeutics to suppress blister formation in the exfoliative toxins-mediated skin disorders, bullous impetio and staphylocccocal scalded-sin syndrome.

exfoliative toxin induces skin blistering by disrupting desmosomal adhesion, and this occurs through a novel mechanism that depends on plakoglobin sequestering and destabilization of other desmosomal cadhernins.
ectodomain-truncated Dsg1, which is generated by bacterial exfoliative toxins, causes blister formation by disrupting desmosomes.
